Apple stage by stage
Apple growers in the hills face trees dying in the orchard, low production and poor fruit, while costs rise every year. Many of these problems start in the root zone and build up over seasons.
Main growing areas: Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir.
Dormancy
Winter
Pruning, orchard cleaning and soil work. Chilling hours decide how well buds break in spring.
Bud break and flowering
Spring
Even bud break and good pollination set the crop. Frost and poor pollination reduce fruit set.
Fruit growth
Summer
Fruit size, colour and firmness build up. Water, balanced nutrition and leaf health matter most.
After harvest
Autumn
The tree stores food for next year. Leaf health after harvest matters for next season's buds.
Common apple problems
Problems farmers bring to us
Trees dying in the orchard
Root rot and collar rot
Low production
Small, poorly coloured fruit
Rising input costs
What to check first
Dig near a weak tree and look at the roots: healthy roots are white and firm, rotting roots are brown and soft.
Check drainage: water standing around trunks invites root rot.
Look at the collar (where trunk meets soil) for cankers.
Test the soil for pH and organic carbon.

Banana stage by stage

Banana grows fast and feeds heavily. In Central Gujarat growers brought us wilt and leaf spot problems, plant losses and poor bunch weight. Soil health, clean planting material and balanced nutrition all matter.
Main growing areas: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.
Planting and establishment
About the first 2 to 3 months
Disease-free suckers or tissue-culture plants and good drainage set the plantation up.
Vegetative growth
About 3 to 7 months
The plant builds leaves; the number of healthy leaves decides bunch size later.
Shooting and bunch
About 7 to 10 months
The bunch emerges and fills. Healthy leaves, water and potash matter most.
Harvest
About 11 to 14 months
Bunch weight and finger quality depend on how the plant was fed all season.
Common banana problems
Wilt (Panama disease)
Leaf spot (Sigatoka)
Plants dying
Low bunch weight
Poor finger size and quality
Use disease-free planting material.
Look for yellowing that starts on older leaves and a split, discoloured stem, which point to wilt.
Remove badly spotted leaves.
Keep drainage good; banana hates standing water.

Citrus stage by stage

Citrus orchards (lemon, lime, sweet orange, mandarin) often suffer from dieback, where branches dry from the tip back, along with fruit drop and declining trees. Roots and drainage are usually where the trouble starts.
Main growing areas: Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.
Flowering
Depends on bahar (season)
Water stress followed by irrigation triggers flowering. Even flowering gives an even crop.
Fruit set
After flowering
Some drop is natural. Heavy drop follows stress or poor nutrition.
Fruit size and juice need steady water and nutrition.
Rest
Between crops
Pruning dead wood and feeding the tree for the next bahar.
Common citrus problems
Dieback of branches
Fruit drop
Yellowing leaves
Trees declining
Check drainage and look at the roots.
Look for gummosis at the trunk base.
Check for zinc and iron shortage: yellow leaves with green veins.
Test soil pH; citrus struggles in very alkaline soil.

Potato guide
Fewer, smaller tubers and rising fertilizer bills.
Photo coming sooncrop-potato-hero.webpWide photo of a healthy potato crop in the field, ideally with the farmer, in Punjab
Potato stage by stage

Potato is a short, heavy-feeding crop. Many growers now use more fertilizer every season but get fewer tubers, smaller sizes and weaker skins. The cause is often below the ground: tired soil and weak roots at the moment tubers are forming.
Main growing areas: Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Gujarat.
Planting and emergence
About the first 3 to 4 weeks
Seed tubers sprout and roots start. Seed quality, soil moisture and soil temperature decide how evenly plants come up.
Leaves and stems build the plant's food factory. Strong roots now support more tubers later.
Tuber initiation
About 6 to 8 weeks
The plant decides how many tubers it will carry. Stress at this stage (water, heat, nutrient shortage) means fewer tubers.
Bulking and maturity
About 8 weeks to harvest
Tubers grow in size and weight, then the skin sets. Steady water and potash matter most.
Common potato problems
Fewer tubers per plant
Small or uneven tubers
Weak skin, poor keeping quality
Fertilizer use going up every season
Use certified, healthy seed tubers of the right size.
Test the soil before planting; potato land often has high salts or low organic carbon.
Avoid water stress at tuber initiation.
Dig a few plants at 7 to 8 weeks and count the tubers set.

Sugarcane guide
Poor germination, gaps, uneven growth and worn-out soil.
Sugarcane stage by stage

Sugarcane stays in the field for a year or more, and the same land often grows it again and again. Over decades this wears the soil out. Growers then see poor germination, gaps in the row, uneven growth and weak ratoons, even with new varieties and more fertilizer.
Main growing areas: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh.
Planting and germination
Setts need moist, airy soil and healthy buds. Poor germination, sett rot and gaps show up here. Gaps filled late never catch up.
About 6 weeks to 4 months
The number of tillers decides the number of millable canes. Weak roots, compacted soil and early water stress reduce tillering.
Grand growth
About 4 to 9 months
Canes put on height and weight. The crop needs steady water and balanced nutrition. Lodging and pests matter most now.
Maturity and ratoon
About 9 months onward
Sugar builds up in the cane. After harvest, stubble care and soil health decide how good the ratoon will be.
Common sugarcane problems
Poor germination and gaps
Plants dying after germination
Uneven growth
Weak ratoons
Soil hard and tired after years of sugarcane
More fertilizer every year for the same yield
Get a soil test: organic carbon, pH and salts (EC) tell you a lot about tired land.
Use healthy, fresh setts from a good nursery.
Look at the roots of weak plants: are they short, brown or few?
Note where gaps are: low spots and hard patches point to water and soil structure problems.

Why is my sugarcane germination poor?

Gujarat Bio Organics is an organic fertilizer and bio fertilizer manufacturer in Gujarat, and one of the fertilizer manufacturing companies of Bhavnagar district, with its own factory in Shihor.

Gujarat Bio Organics started in 2006 in Bhavnagar, Gujarat. From the beginning the work has been on real farms: walking fields with growers, finding out why a crop was failing, and building formulas that solve those problems.
That work led to the Immunity range: Specials for 20 crops, formulas for all crops, 11 biofertilizers and soil granules.
What we make
Biostimulants, our main line: humic and fulvic acid, seaweed extracts, amino acids and protein hydrolysates
Biofertilizers: nitrogen fixers, phosphate, potash and zinc solubilisers, mycorrhiza and consortia
Organic fertilizers and the Immunity crop formulas
How we make it

Everything is made at our own factory in Shihor, Bhavnagar. Nearly 20 years of field work have taught us which raw materials work. We extract them in-house without harsh chemicals, very high pH or heat, because the helpful substances in humus and seaweed are fragile.
What we believe
We want to make farming free of hazardous chemicals and make sustainable food growing easier for the generations to come.
Founder
Gafar Laiya founded Gujarat Bio Organics and leads its product development and farmer programmes. He writes many of the guides on this site.

Eliminate hunger

Healthier soil
Every Immunity formula is made to work with living soil. Our biofertilizers add helpful microbes and our granules improve soil structure.
Fewer hazardous chemicals
Our mission is to make farming free of hazardous chemicals. Healthier crops on healthier soil need less rescue spraying.

Micronutrients in agriculture: what they are, how they work and why they matter

Micronutrients are the nutrients a crop needs in very small amounts: zinc, iron, manganese, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel. They switch on the enzymes, hormones and processes that let the crop use nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, form chlorophyll, flower, set fruit and resist stress. A shortage of any one limits the whole crop, however much NPK is applied, and Indian soil tests show such shortages are widespread.

What are micronutrients?

Plants need 17 essential nutrients. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from air and water. The rest come from the soil and fall into groups by how much the crop needs. Micronutrients, also called trace elements, are needed in grams per acre rather than kilograms, but a crop cannot complete its life without them.

How micronutrients work
They switch on enzymes: zinc, manganese, copper, iron, molybdenum and nickel are parts of, or activators for, enzymes that drive growth and energy.
They make chlorophyll possible: iron and manganese are needed to form it and run photosynthesis; magnesium sits at its centre.
They make hormones: zinc is needed for auxin, the growth hormone.
They build cell walls: boron and calcium hold walls together, and silicon strengthens them.
They make flowers fertile: boron, zinc and copper are needed for pollen and seed set.
They help use nitrogen: molybdenum, nickel and sulphur turn nitrogen into protein; molybdenum and cobalt help legumes fix it.
They defend the crop: copper, manganese, boron and silicon strengthen tissue against pests and disease.

India's soils: shortages are widespread

An ICAR survey of 2,42,827 soil samples from 615 districts found 58.6% of soils short of sulphur, 51.2% of zinc, 44.7% of boron, 19.2% of iron, 17.4% of manganese and 11.4% of copper, counting hidden shortages. Many fields were short of two or three nutrients together, most often sulphur with zinc, zinc with boron and sulphur with boron. Alkaline and calcareous soils, low organic matter and years of urea, DAP and MOP without sulphur or micronutrients are the main reasons.

Indian soil figures: Shukla AK, Behera SK and others (2021). Deficiency of phyto-available sulphur, zinc, boron, iron, copper and manganese in soils of India. Scientific Reports 11, 19760. Based on 2,42,827 soil samples from 615 districts in 28 states. Read the study. The figures include soils with a hidden (latent) shortage.
Common practices that miss the cause
Applying more urea when leaves turn yellow, though yellowing from sulphur, iron, zinc or magnesium does not respond to nitrogen.
Using NPK water-soluble fertilizer as a cure-all, though most grades carry little or no micronutrient.
Spraying a pesticide when the crop looks weak, even when no pest is present.
Treating the nutrient that shows the symptom, when the real limit is another nutrient, the soil pH or the water supply.

What are micronutrients in agriculture?

Nutrients a crop needs in very small amounts: zinc, iron, manganese, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel. Calcium, magnesium and sulphur are secondary nutrients, and silicon and cobalt are beneficial elements.
What is the difference between micronutrients and trace elements?
In farming the two terms are used for the same group: nutrients needed only in trace amounts. Trace elements is sometimes also used for beneficial elements such as cobalt and selenium.
Which micronutrient is most deficient in Indian soils?
Among micronutrients, zinc, followed by boron. Sulphur, a secondary nutrient, is even more widely short.
Can NPK alone give a good crop?
Only if the soil supplies enough of every other nutrient. Where a micronutrient is short, more NPK does not lift the yield.
How do I know which micronutrient my crop needs?
Read the leaf symptoms, rule out pests and disease, and confirm with a soil and leaf test.

Zinc (Zn) in crops: role, deficiency signs and how to correct it

Zinc is a micronutrient the crop needs for its growth hormone (auxin), for more than a hundred enzymes, for chlorophyll and for healthy pollen. A zinc-short crop has small, narrow, pale new leaves, short internodes and poor tillering or flowering. Zinc is the most common micronutrient shortage in Indian soils, especially in alkaline, calcareous and low organic matter fields.

What zinc does in the plant
Helps the plant make auxin, the hormone that drives cell growth and normal leaf size.
Switches on many enzymes for energy, protein building and sugar use.
Needed for chlorophyll formation, so the leaf stays green.
Keeps cell membranes healthy, which helps roots hold nutrients and resist stress.
Supports pollen and seed formation, so it matters at flowering and grain fill.
How zinc moves in the plant

Zinc moves only a little inside the plant, so a shortage shows first on young and middle leaves. Once a leaf is formed short of zinc, it does not recover; only the new growth after correction looks normal.
Signs of zinc deficiency
Pale or yellow patches between the veins of young leaves, while veins stay green.
Small, narrow leaves, often bunched at the tip (little leaf or rosetting).
Short internodes, so the plant looks stunted and bushy.
Rusty brown spots on older leaves of paddy a few weeks after transplanting.
A white or pale band on both sides of the midrib in young maize leaves.
Delayed flowering and maturity, poor grain filling.

Where and why it happens
In India, an ICAR survey of more than two lakh soil samples found 51.2% of soils short of zinc, counting hidden shortages.
Alkaline and calcareous soils, common in Saurashtra and much of Gujarat.
Soils low in organic matter.
Fields where the topsoil was removed in land levelling.
Heavy, repeated use of phosphate fertilizers such as DAP.
Flooded paddy soils.
Cold, wet weather early in the season, which slows root uptake.
Sandy soils that are low in zinc to start with.
How it works with other nutrients
High phosphorus can lower zinc uptake, so DAP-heavy fields often show zinc shortage.
In high pH and calcareous soils zinc becomes less available.
Very high zinc can lower iron uptake.
Nitrogen raises the crop's need for zinc, so a well-fed crop shows zinc shortage sooner.

What happens if it is not managed
Stunted plants and fewer tillers or branches.
Late and weak flowering, poor fruit and grain set.
Lower grain weight and a poorer harvest even when NPK was applied.
Grain and fodder with less zinc, which matters for people and animals who eat them.
See the full picture of what unmanaged shortages cost.
How to confirm it
Look at the youngest leaves first: small, narrow, pale leaves point to zinc.
Rule out pests, virus and herbicide drift, which can look similar.
Ask for a DTPA zinc soil test, which is part of the Soil Health Card test.
A leaf test at the right stage confirms what the crop actually took up.
Spray a small strip and compare the new growth after one to two weeks.
How to correct it
Soil application of zinc sulphate before or at sowing in deficient fields. Do not mix it with phosphate fertilizers in the same bag or tank.
Foliar spray of zinc sulphate or a chelated zinc on the standing crop for quick correction of new growth.
Zinc-coated urea or zincated fertilizers where available.
Seed or seedling root dip for crops where your agriculture department advises it.
Zinc solubilising bacteria and organic manure to free zinc already locked in the soil and keep it available.
Take the dose from your soil test report, the product label or your agriculture officer.
Too much zinc
Zinc excess is rare in fields. It can happen near industrial waste or after repeated heavy doses.
Too much zinc can cause iron shortage, seen as yellow young leaves.

What is the main sign of zinc deficiency?
Small, narrow, pale young leaves with short internodes. In paddy, rusty brown spots a few weeks after transplanting (khaira) are a classic sign.
Why is zinc deficiency common in Gujarat?
Many soils in Gujarat are alkaline and calcareous and low in organic matter. Zinc becomes less available in these conditions.
Can I mix zinc sulphate with DAP?
Avoid mixing them in the same bag or tank. Phosphate and zinc can react, and high phosphorus also lowers zinc uptake.
Is foliar or soil application better for zinc?

Soil application builds up the field for the season. Foliar spray corrects the new growth quickly. Many growers use soil application where a soil test shows deficiency and foliar spray to correct a standing crop.
How quickly does a zinc spray work?
New leaves formed after the spray are normal in size and colour. Old damaged leaves do not recover.

Iron (Fe) in crops: role, deficiency signs and how to correct it

Iron is a micronutrient the crop needs to make chlorophyll and to run photosynthesis and respiration. An iron-short crop shows yellow young leaves with a fine net of green veins, and in severe cases the new leaves turn almost white. Iron shortage is usually not a lack of iron in the soil but iron locked up in alkaline, calcareous or waterlogged soils.

Why are the new leaves yellow but the old leaves green?
Iron does not move from old leaves to new ones. Yellow young leaves with green veins usually point to iron shortage.
My soil has plenty of iron. Why is the crop iron deficient?
In alkaline, calcareous or waterlogged soils, iron is present but locked up. The crop cannot take it up, so the problem is availability, not quantity.
Does ferrous sulphate in the soil work?
In calcareous soil it is often locked up quickly. Foliar sprays or iron chelates made for high pH soils usually work better.
Can overwatering cause yellow leaves?
Yes. Waterlogged roots cannot take up iron, so the crop yellows even when iron is present.
